welcome

by the end of this blended course, you will be able to do the following: understand vocabulary development and spelling-meaning connections. analyze vocabulary assessments to identify students’ needs and organize for instruction. determine how best to instruct students using generative and word-specific strategies. select appropriate instructional strategies and activities to expand students’ academic vocabulary.

english: shakespearean sonnet science: lab report math: textbook social studies: political cartoon after you have compared the vocabulary demands of each discipline’s text, reflect on the following question in the participant workbook: if you were to ask your students to describe how an expert in your field reads or writes, what might they say? use the guiding questions in your participant workbook to help you compare vocabulary demands within the text types from four disciplines. (templeton et al. 2010, 102)
learn
text-based support: evidence from a text or set of texts used to enhance, prove, or reinforce ideas in written or oral communication
student writing task student writing sample

let’s think about the writer’s use of textual support and disciplinary vocabulary. this essay provides evidence from "giving faces to the lost," which is explicitly cited. it is unclear whether the writer incorporated evidence from other texts. the writer explains several steps for their investigation, such as examining tattoos, piercings, and scars; however, the writer does not provide evidence for why they might conduct this step. the writer includes accurate disciplinary vocabulary, such as biological profile, facial reconstruction, and forensic odontologist.

the writer also uses transitions that are appropriate to the content and help to clarify the relationship among ideas. for example, "once i got to the lab the first thing i must find out is…” or “i soon discovered that…" overall, the writer has done a nice job of incorporating disciplinary vocabulary. it seems as if the writer may be using more text-based support than he or she is actually citing. the teacher may want to work with this writer to develop his or her explanations with concrete details and relevant evidence. this would include supporting the writer to name the texts or sources of information that he or she references.

sample a sample b now it is your turn! you will evaluate two additional student writing samples from the task we just read about. in your participant workbook, you will compare the two writing samples and determine future instructional steps based on the writing samples. click on student writing sample a and student writing sample b to read each sample.

as the name suggests, text-dependent questions require a dependence on text to provide an answer. these kinds of questions require an understanding beyond life experiences and basic recall of facts. providing students with good text-dependent questions will help them analyze the text, investigate its meaning, and develop a deep understanding of the text. when we ask students text-dependent questions, we put students in the position to use disciplinary vocabulary in their responses. sample questions

mr. hanstead is teaching a unit about the american dream. students have just read dr. martin luther king jr.’s “i have a dream” speech. mr. hanstead asks students the following questions. determine which questions are text-dependent questions. how would you describe your own american dream? when martin luther king jr. says, “the life of the negro is still sadly crippled by the manacles of segregation and the chains of discrimination,” what is he referring to? look for words or phrases that are repetitious in the speech. why do you think martin luther king jr. uses repetition? why does he repeat these particular words what is the emancipation proclamation? analyze the use of pronouns in the speech. when martin luther king jr. refers to “we” and “my people” who is he referring to? how do you know this? do you think that the world we live in today is a reflection of martin luther king jr.’s dream?

how would you describe your own american dream? students could answer this question without reading the speech. it draws on opinions and doesn’t ask students to look to the text. this is not a text-dependent question.

time for a quick-check! respond to the text-dependent questioning quick-check questions in your participant workbook. why is the following question not a text-dependent question? after romeo went to visit the friar, what did he do next? what is the value of asking students text-dependent questions?

look for words or phrases that are repetitious in the speech. why do you think martin luther king jr. uses repetition? why does he repeat these particular words or phrases? this question requires students to analyze the organization and rhetoric of the speech. students will need to reflect on the overall meaning in order to determine why particular words or phrases are repeated. this is a text-dependent question.

what is the emancipation proclamation? although the emancipation proclamation is mentioned in the speech, students may be able to answer this question from their background knowledge. also, although the speech mentions the emancipation proclamation, it does not define it or provide information about it. this is not a text-dependent question.

when martin luther king jr. says, “the life of the negro is still sadly crippled by the manacles of segregation and the chains of discrimination,” what is he referring to? this question asks students to go back and reread a section of text to deeply analyze the meaning of a phrase. asking the question this way sets students up for using vocabulary as they answer the question. students may need to read around the phrase to determine the meaning. this is a text-dependent question.

do you think that the world we live in today is a reflection of martin luther king jr.’s dream? to answer this question, students will likely draw evidence from their life experiences and knowledge of what the world is like today. although students could refer back to the speech to compare his dream to current affairs, the question is not set up in a way that requires them to do so. if this question was reworded to include an emphasis on drawing conclusions about the american dream from the text, it could be a text-dependent question.

analyze the use of pronouns in the speech. when martin luther king jr. refers to “we” and “my people” who is he referring to? how do you know this? this question requires students to reread the text specifically to analyze pronoun use, and it also requires them to reflect on the message of the speech or analysis of some sections to determine the antecedents of the pronouns. this is a text-dependent question.

after reading “i have a dream,” mr. hanstead’s students work in groups to explore some of the deeper issues inherent in the speech. students will begin writing an argumentative essay shortly, and their work in groups will help prepare them for that task. using text-dependent questions, mr. hanstead provides each group with a focus for their discussion. students will collaboratively write responses to the questions. mr. hanstead wants students to use disciplinary vocabulary and provide text-based support, so he decides to provide a scaffold to assist students as they craft sophisticated responses. he models the use of several sentence frames that will help students get started.

in ______(the text), _______(the author) ______(active verb) ____________________. in “i have a dream,” martin luther king jr. communicates his hope that america will evolve into a nation that has achieved equality and done so in a peaceful manner. in ____(the text), _____(the author) writes, “_____.” he/she is ____(active verb) _____________. in “i have a dream,” martin luther king jr. writes, “we refuse to believe that there are insufficient funds in the great vaults of opportunity of this nation.” he is comparing the value of freedom to the value of funds in a bank…

in your participant workbook, reflect on the use of sentence frames. think about a recent writing activity or assignment that was part of your instruction. what kind of sentence frame could you provide for that activity or assignment?
teacher modeling and guided practice are other important instructional strategies to promote students’ use of disciplinary vocabulary in their writing.
in practice

take a look at this instruction in practice. during this video, you will observe a lesson in which the teacher uses sentence frames, modeling, and guided practice to help her students become comfortable using disciplinary vocabulary and text-based support. click the video to begin. use the participant workbook to take notes on the teacher’s use of strategies.
in the participant workbook, use the last column of the chart to describe your experiences with the strategies and your level of comfort in using the strategies going forward.
apply

a colleague approaches you in the teacher’s lounge with a stack of student essays. with a grimace on his face, he drops the stack of essays on the table and begins to share his disappointment about the students’ essays. he shares with you that 50% of each student’s grade is based on their textual support. unfortunately, very few students incorporated any textual support into their essay. the teacher recognizes that the essays are evidence that he failed to prepare students for this task.

you ask your colleague what his instruction on using text-based support was like. he mentions a detailed handout with a lot of examples that he went through over the course of a few class periods. he also had students highlight areas of each text that they felt they could use as evidence in the essay. your colleague asks you what you would have done, or what you suggest he does going forward. he plans on having students rewrite or revise the essays after further instruction. what suggestions might you give your colleague? in the participant workbook, craft your response back to your colleague.

your students have just finished reading romeo and juliet and subsequently wrote an essay explaining which character they felt was responsible for the death of romeo and juliet, using text-based support. while reading the play, you modeled the use of text-based support by writing mini-essays in class at the end of each act. students also practiced text-based support in their discussions, as well as in short writing assignments.

additionally, you worked with a small group of students who needed extra support and provided them with some sentence frames to use in their essay. overall you were extremely pleased with students’ essays. with a few exceptions, students were able to use text-based support to prove their argument in their essay. one of your students, melinda, was upset by her grade. she is an “a” student and writing comes naturally to her. although her essay was well-crafted, she didn’t provide text-based support to back up her ideas. she ended up with a c+ grade on her essay.

you spoke with melinda after school and reviewed the grading rubric to make sure that she understood her score. you also showed her an anonymous student sample that contained strong textual support so that she could see how her essay was different. you receive an e-mail from melinda’s parents expressing their frustration over her score. they understand the rubric, but they don’t think that the use of text-based support is important or worthy of so many points. in the participant workbook, craft a reply e-mail for melinda’s parents explaining why the use of text-based support is important and respond to their concern over their daughter’s score.
reflect

take out the student writing samples that you brought. read through them to identify any use of text-based support or disciplinary vocabulary. in the participant workbook, reflect on how you want your instruction to change to support students’ use of text-based support and disciplinary vocabulary. record any questions that you still have in the still wondering section of your participant workbook. you will have a chance to ask these questions to the facilitator in the live session later on in the course. ? ? ?

by the end of this blended course, you will be able to do the following: understand vocabulary development and spelling-meaning connections. analyze vocabulary assessments to identify students’ needs and organize for instruction. determine how best to instruct students using generative and word-specific strategies. select appropriate instructional strategies and activities to expand students’ academic vocabulary. today, we focused primarily on these outcomes.
look forward

to apply what you have learned and engage in a professional discussion, respond to the discussion questions on the discussion board. remember to respond to at least two participants’ posts in addition to posting your own response to each question.
in preparation for next session, do the following: select and bring a complex text that students often struggle to comprehend. read the article excerpt “building capacity through close reading.”
